extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy (educated readers of Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory exposition of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, outlining what counts as the good life, the nature and formation of virtue, responsibility, practical wisdom, justice, pleasure, friendship, and the role of the state in moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as the highest end (telos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of all action is the greatest happiness (welfare or well-being); the good toward which all human desires and activities are directed is Happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is the supreme end and object of desire for individuals and the state; it is not merely physical pleasure, wealth, or honor. The text rejects identifications of the good with mere pleasures, political power, or wealth. Understanding the end is practically important as it guides life and legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness consists in activity in accordance with virtue/reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Human happiness lies in activity or energising, specifically activity characteristic of man—practical activity involving reason—and presupposing development of relevant powers and capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is an active exercise of capacities (not merely possession). It is practical rather than purely theoretical, though length of life, wealth, and luck affect attainability. The highest form identified later is contemplative activity, but practical virtuous activity is central for most people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: virtues of intellect vs virtues of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual virtues are excellences of reason (acquired by study and instruction); virtues of character are acquired by discipline and habituation and govern passions and impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two kinds are different in origin and function but interrelate: intellectual virtues concern knowing and formulating rules; moral virtues concern regulating instincts and feelings. Both excite admiration and are acquired, not innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtues are acquired by habituation (formation of character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character (good or bad) is produced by habituation—the repeated doing of acts of a similar quality, which, acting on natural aptitudes, fix a bias toward good or evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formation of good character requires discipline, imitation, and external direction; mere intellectual instruction is insufficient. Repetition makes right acts easier and pleasant until they become 'second nature' and the agent does them willingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the Mean (virtue as mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: Right action or feeling in a situation is doing or feeling the right amount—not more or less; moral virtue lies between excess and deficiency (each virtue is flanked by two vices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rightness is adaptation to the special requirements of the situation; the exact mean must be determined by intuition in each individual case. The doctrine is a principle of arrangement for virtues but application is context-sensitive and not a strict mechanical rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtue as a stable state of the agent (obedience to rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral virtue is a permanent state of the agent—a steady, self-imposed obedience to a rule of action in recurrent situations—rather than a mere mood, liability to emotion, or natural endowment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule prescribes control and regulation of natural impulses within limits. Virtue permits variety within its limits; conformity requires inner consent and is not successfully described as simple mechanical uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rules are general and admit exceptions; lack mathematical precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral or practical rules are general, state probabilities rather than certainties, admit exceptions, and are deficient in exactness compared to mathematical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human conduct is not governed by necessary uniform laws; practical knowledge requires experience as source and test. One must not look for a mathematics of conduct; rules serve as guides amid unpredictable variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral knowledge requires moral experience and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: True understanding and profitable application of moral principles presuppose moral experience—the actual possession and exercise of good character—rather than mere intellectual apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual apprehension alone is often profitless; experience is necessary both to test principles and to form the capacity to apply them in particular situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness, deliberation, choice, and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done under coercion or through ignorance of relevant circumstances are involuntary and exempt from responsibility; voluntary acts (especially deliberate acts of choice) imply deliberation and inner consent and thus responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation involves thinking about means to ends; deliberate acts are 'his' in a peculiar sense—they express the agent's character. Neither mere passion nor ignorance of the right rule excuses responsibility, though metaphysical issues about will are acknowledged as difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a civic moral virtue; distributive vs corrective justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice (in the restricted civic sense) is the special goodness of character required of the adult citizen for the administration of civic life; distributive justice concerns allocation of gains, corrective justice concerns legal redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats justice as a habit producible by discipline. His distinctions are pragmatic and limited in scope (focused on civic functions). Attempts to give precise mathematical forms to principles of justice are criticized as confusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical wisdom (phronesis) and its interdependence with moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodness of intellect has theoretical and practical forms; practical wisdom (the supreme practical intellectual virtue) supplies right rules of conduct and presupposes formed moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical wisdom enables a person to produce the right rule at once and to justify it by connection to the end. It depends on a clear apprehension of the end and on experience; without moral virtue it degenerates into mere 'cleverness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The reality and difficulty of incontinence (weakness of will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incontinence is the phenomenon where someone knows or acknowledges the good but repeatedly fails to act on it—a divided will where desire overmasters reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats the condition as involving some rational element in desires (especially bodily pleasures) and acknowledges the problem's complexity; he does not offer a full solution but analyses motives and conflict between reason and appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as concomitant and index of activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is the natural concomitant and index of perfect activity: distinguishable but inseparable from activity at its best, and always in itself a good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure's value rises and falls with the worth of the activity it accompanies; the highest pleasures are those accompanying the highest activities. Pleasure is necessary in the best life but not its entirety or principal ingredient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplative life as highest form of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest and most satisfying life possible to man is the contemplative life—the life of philosophical and scientific contemplation—rather than the purely practical or political life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contemplative ideal is lofty but criticized for being obscure in relation to the practical ideal, accessible to few, and perhaps unnecessarily limited in content. Nevertheless it is presented as the supreme form of happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the State and Law in producing good character
rubrics_metrics.description: The political community (the State), chiefly through law and institutions, is the main educative agency for producing good character and enabling the best life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle assigns to legislation and political organisation a central role in fostering virtues and expanding individual opportunities. The Ethics is complementary to the Politics, which will address how law and institutions should be constituted to secure good character.
